speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: asked the Minister for Education in light of the forthcoming merger of the Yale-NUS College and NUS’ University Scholars Programme (USP) (a) how will the establishment of the New College enhance the educational experience of future students as compared to the current programmes at Yale-NUS College and USP; and (b) how will the decision affect the (i) innovative and open liberal arts curriculum (ii) international make-up of the students and the faculty of the New College and (iii) higher education offerings in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: asked the Minister for Education whether support can be provided to students who have accepted an offer for the cohort starting 2022-2023 in NUS' Yale-NUS College, Faculty of Engineering or School of Design and Environment but who wish to change University or school given the recent merger announcements.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) what are the considerations for the forthcoming merger of the Yale-NUS College and the University Scholars Programme; (b) what measures will be taken by the Ministry to safeguard the interests of the existing students; and (c) what are the plans for the future college.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked the Minister for Education in light of the closure of Yale-NUS College (a) how will this impact the quality of education for the students; and (b) what will be done to address potential concerns about credibility of the degree and post-graduate opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Minister for Education in light of the announcement that Yale-NUS College will cease operations by 2025 (a) how will NUS ensure that students enrolled over the course of the next four years will be able to enjoy an uncompromised educational experience; (b) whether there will be any reduction of fees or option for transfers in the event that there is a compromised experience; and (c) how will NUS ensure that the Yale-NUS degree retains its value in the future, in particular for graduates of the programme.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) whether he can shed light on (i) the decision-making process behind the merger of Yale-NUS College and NUS’ University Scholars Programme (USP) and (ii) the potential implications on collaboration between NUS and other foreign universities; and (b) whether NUS will provide refunds to Yale-NUS College and USP students who prefer to withdraw.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: USP started as one of NUS’ early ventures in offering a broad-based, interdisciplinary education to students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ten years ago, NUS and Yale University established YNC.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The aim was to establish a new unique education model that draws on the best traditions of both the East and the West, with a multidisciplinary curriculum.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: YNC has an intake of about 250 students each year.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: More than 800 students have graduated from YNC thus far.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is autonomous within NUS, but as part of the wider NUS family, it taps on the resources and facilities of NUS.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This decade-long partnership with Yale University has given NUS valuable insights into interdisciplinary liberal arts education and its defining features such as the integration of residential living and learning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Over these years, the rest of NUS too has continued to evolve and innovate to remain relevant to the needs of our students and country.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, NUS is one of the leading universities in Asia and the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And in one international ranking, the QS World University Rankings, NUS is ranked 11th in the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, NUS, like all our other universities, cannot remain static in the face of a changing and in many ways, more challenging world; NUS will have to continue to evolve.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, in our quest for excellence, it means that we must continue to learn from the best internationally, while charting our own path forward with confidence.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is what brought us thus far; and this is how we will go forward.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In a more complex, uncertain and even fragmenting world, our universities must enable our students: (a) to be more global in orientation and exposure, able to connect the East and West; North and South; (b) to be more able to solve complex issues with greater interdisciplinarity and versatility, connecting various disciplines, from STEM to the Arts; and (c) to be more confident of our own value in creating new ideas in context, for Singapore and the world beyond.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Against this backdrop, NUS has charted a bold roadmap of educational innovations since 2018, geared towards delivering a common curriculum with more flexible pathways and more interdisciplinary learning, to develop in students greater intellectual versatility.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Part of this roadmap includes the establishment of the College of Humanities and Sciences (CHS) in December 2020, which brought together two of NUS’ largest faculties to offer students multiple pathways across the Humanities, Social Sciences, and Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will be followed by the establishment of the College of Design and Engineering (CDE) which will similarly transform the experience of our engineering, architecture and design students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The New College is a third important step in this roadmap.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It was motivated by NUS’ vision of further developing an immersive living and learning community, where students majoring in over 50 different disciplines can come together to inquire, interact and learn from one another.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: YNC and USP share many common features, including smaller group teaching, a common curriculum and residential living and learning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Both YNC and USP graduates go on to enjoy similarly excellent employment outcomes, contributing in different sectors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The New College will bring together the best educational features of both YNC and USP.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With the New College more fully integrated with the rest of the University ecosystem, its students will benefit from greater exposure to a wider range of disciplines compared to just YNC alone.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The cost of education of a YNC student today is more than double that of a Humanities or Science student in NUS.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Likewise, both tuition fees and Government funding are more than double.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we accepted this because we saw value in having a liberal arts college in our tertiary education system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This would then have reduced the burden on the annual operating income of fees and Government subsidies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: YNC has done its utmost in raising funds, but through no fault of its own, has not reached its target.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Transitioning to the New College will give us economies of scale and reduce costs to some extent.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will be an important consideration but not the main motivation for the change.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: NUS has learnt much from its partnership with Yale and in operating YNC, and it has affirmed the value of a liberal arts educational approach.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The launch of the New College is an important move.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It has also implications for many stakeholders, not least for the YNC community of students, parents, faculty and staff.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I understand the sadness and sense of loss and uncertainty they may feel, especially for those who have played a part in building up YNC over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Allow me to address the decision-making process and how students and all the affected stakeholders will be supported.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, the decision-making process and the timing of the announcement.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Yale acknowledged NUS’ vision to bring together both YNC and USP into a New College that would not bear Yale’s name.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The YNC leadership was informed in the same month.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The NUS Board of Trustees endorsed the decision in early-August 2021 and the YNC Governing Board endorsed the transition plans in late-August.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In July, the issue of timing was also discussed with Yale and jointly determined.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While the partnership would only end in 2025, both parties felt that the responsible thing to do was to announce it early rather than to hold back.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It would have been bad faith to delay the announcement and continue to admit students who would not be able to complete their education in YNC, or to continue to hire faculty, beyond this juncture.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The announcement was thus planned for August, after the YNC Governing Board considered and endorsed the broad transition approach.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some have also asked why was there no consultation with the current student body and staff.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: NUS did not do so because the decision involved discussions between the senior leadership of two Universities and with their respective Boards, on sensitive issues of strategy and finance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Instead, NUS, once having settled the broad parameters, wanted to give maximum time for the transition to occur and for the stakeholders to be involved in working through the transition issues.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, students, parents and alumni have asked how the move affects the stature of the YNC degree.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, YNC graduates graduate with a YNC degree that is awarded by NUS itself.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: NUS and Yale are both globally renowned universities which are well-recognised by employers, including the public sector and postgraduate institutions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am confident that the YNC degree will continue to be highly valued and its past and future graduating cohorts will remain in good standing, even beyond 2025.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Beyond 2025, NUS will continue to provide supporting documentation to explain the context of YNC and what a YNC degree conveys, and provide letters of recommendation or referees if alumni need them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, concerns around how the merger will affect current students, faculty and staff.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students in YNC will continue to have access to the full range of majors and minors currently offered by YNC until 2025.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I know that many YNC students are actively involved in student organisations and look forward to a fulfilling campus life during their time at the College.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The establishment of the New College will open new possibilities for students of YNC, USP and the New College to interact and collectively participate in active and inclusive student life in the next few years.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: YNC is an autonomous institution under NUS; YNC faculty and staff have been and remain part of the NUS family.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: NUS has committed to honouring all existing employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: YNC leadership have been engaging faculty members to hear their concerns and discuss possible options for faculty members after the merger takes full effect in 2025, four years ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The YNC Governing Board, comprising NUS and Yale University leadership, will continue to steward the College until its transition in 2025.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I know some students and parents may, nevertheless, have lingering concerns and we respect the preferences of those who may wish to consider other options.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: NUS and YNC will engage them and provide assistance where they can.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: NUS is, in fact, building on the foundations of YNC and USP, as well as the lessons gleaned from the collaboration with Yale University.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It wants to make the distinctive feature of education in YNC and USP more inclusive and more accessible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The New College will maintain the spirit of independent inquiry and inclusivity that characterise YNC, USP and NUS.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some have asked about the impact of the merger on academic freedom in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On this topic, I would like to make two points.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, there had been similar concerns about a perceived lack of academic freedom when YNC was established.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, few believed then that YNC would live up to its ambition.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is, perhaps, ironic and a testimony to NUS and YNC’s efforts all these years, that YNC is now seen as a paragon of academic freedom in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, YNC's current policies on academic freedom were, in fact, framed by taking reference from NUS' practices relating to academic freedom and these practices have remained unchanged since.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Faculties of Arts and Social Sciences in NUS and other Autonomous Universities also have had a long history of teaching and research, including on potentially sensitive and difficult topics, long before the establishment of YNC.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They are highly ranked globally and attract distinguished scholars.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It would be grossly unfair to faculty members in NUS and other Autonomous Universities to suggest that their teaching or research is in any way less rigorous, of lower quality or less free than that of the YNC faculty.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Many of our newer institutions were started in partnership with leading global universities, so that we can learn from the best globally.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These partnerships have generally progressed, evolved and matured as intended.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In some cases, they come to a natural end at the checkpoints designed into the initial partnership agreements.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Meanwhile, our universities continue to seek out new partnerships where we can benefit from the experiences of others and where we can value-add to the relationships meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have much more to learn from others, not just from universities in the United States, but equally from Europe, Asia and elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But to be an attractive partner for others, we too must find our own unique value propositions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We cannot and should not be a cloned version of others, no matter how successful they may be.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are also open to exploring other collaboration opportunities with Yale University in the future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members of Parliament have asked how it will improve the overall student experience compared to today and what resources will be invested.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I expect the New College to also have a global orientation and welcome a diversity of international students to forge a vibrant student body.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In setting up the New College, NUS is not starting from scratch.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It will tap on the experiences of the faculty and students of both YNC and USP, and build on their strong foundations and rich traditions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students and faculty from YNC and USP have been invited to be part of the New College planning committee.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am sure they will have much to contribute to make the New College a success.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It would offer a wider choice of majors and minors, particularly in STEM disciplines, compared to YNC, and a student experience that seeks to combine the best features of both YNC and USP.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With closer integration with the wider NUS ecosystem, all NUS students will also be able to benefit from and access the New College’s facilities, resources and community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some have asked whether NUS can deliver this enhanced ambition and whether there will be an impact on its overall standing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There is no reason to believe why a University like NUS, which has grown in strength and reputation over the years, cannot continue to achieve great things.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In closing, Mr Speaker, Sir, the establishment of the New College marks a new chapter in inquiry-driven, interdisciplinary education for NUS and for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The NUS and YNC leadership are committed to supporting the YNC and USP communities through the transition and to making the New College a success.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This move brings exciting new opportunities, so my hope is that we look ahead and move forward together.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Last week, I had the chance to speak with student leaders from YNC and USP.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I listened to their hopes and concerns, and encouraged them to work together on the journey ahead.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have every confidence that we will take forward the legacy, spirit and communities of YNC and USP together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, the Minister mentioned that costs were a relevant consideration but not the main motivation for the merger.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on how the financial sustainability was factored into this consideration and how the New College would be made more financially sustainable?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As YNC is a four-year residential programme, students live in and are part of the residential colleges that are exclusively for YNC students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: YNC students primarily take modules that are offered by YNC but they may opt to take modules that are offered by other NUS faculties.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: YNC's facilities, such as the multi-purpose hall, fitness centre, computer laboratory, study areas and lounges are dedicated to YNC students' use and therefore, only accessible by them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The New College will be more integrated with NUS compared to YNC.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It will not have a separate governing board but will instead have an international advisory panel.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will become clearer as the Planning Committee engages stakeholders and formulates its vision and plans for the New College in due course.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For now, NUS expects the New College to be more inclusive and accessible to students in four ways.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, fees will be lower than YNC fees, making it a more affordable and more attractive option for more students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, the New College can attract students from across a wider range of discipline.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, YNC students who want to benefit from the immersive residential and interdisciplinary experience in YNC can only choose their majors from 14 options.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In future, students from the New College will be able to enjoy immersive residential and interdisciplinary experience and access a whole range of about 50 possible majors across NUS, enabling them to interact with a greater diversity of students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, compared to the USP experience today, the New College students will potentially have a richer residential life component.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And fourth, the New College facilities and resources will be accessible to all NUS students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Planning Committee is now engaging the various stakeholders and I look forward to their report.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second supplementary question by Mr Patrick Tay about the cost issue, let me first reiterate that the overriding reason for this move, as NUS has shared, is the vital role of a broad-based interdisciplinary education and our job to reimagine the higher education and how it will fit into our country's plans going forward so that we can develop a new generation of students that are much more global in their perspective, much more able to connect the East and the West, the North and the South.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When YNC was first established, the Government recognised that education in YNC will cost more because of its smaller size and unique education model.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we were prepared to invest in building the new facilities for YNC and we accepted this because we saw value in having a liberal arts college in our tertiary education system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the specific numbers, on a recurrent basis, YNC is more costly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Beyond the operating grant, MOE has also provided capital funding for YNC's infrastructure and matched donations to YNC's endowment fund.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When NUS consulted MOE on its plan to merge the YNC and USP programmes together to form the New College, we were supportive of this for two reasons.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, because this is in line with our broader push for Institutes of Higher Learning to expand their interdisciplinary approach to education.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, because it will make education much more affordable to many more NUS students in keeping with NUS' ethos and mission as a public university.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Prof Tan Eng Chye, President of NUS has articulated the reasons for the merger in his recent op-ed over the weekend.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think it makes sense for him to have the interests of the wider NUS student population and the whole NUS at the forefront of what he is doing with his leadership team in NUS.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The first is given that the intention is to make the liberal arts education more accessible, how much larger does MOE expect the cohorts to be, given that it is to be noted that the current projected 500-student cohort for the New College is not actually that much bigger than the current combined cohorts of USP and YNC, as well as to what extent will the composition be made up of Singaporeans as well as foreign students?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, given that potential students will be applying for the next admission cycle in the coming months, will MOE guide or require the New College to set out its admission policy and confirmed majors to be offered, for example, so that potential students and parents can make considered decisions, given that this is a fairly short amount of time?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And Minister, if I could just go back to the Question No 13, my original PQ: if MOE will consider facilitating any assistance to those who had to forego other universities in order to take up this offer?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The more interdisciplinary approach to the education system will not be just confined to the 500 students in the New College.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some of the best elements that we have been able to learn from these two traditions is that we will be able to scale this even to students beyond those that are going to be at the New College.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, yes, for a start, I think the Planning Committee is looking at 500 or a bit more for the New College, but there are elements of this that will actually percolate to the rest of the NUS ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Going forward, for the initial planning parameters of the 500, what is the balance between the international and the local students will still have to be decided by the Planning Committee.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would look forward to NUS coming back to us on this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the third issue about the admission policies for the next batch, yes, indeed, NUS is now making clear the offerings for the subsequent batch as early as possible so that they have the maximum time before they sign up for the different courses – for the next batch which will matriculate next year.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the fourth question, yes, NUS will definitely provide assistance to staff and faculty, as I have mentioned, for those who want to make alternative plans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can Members keep to two supplementary questions, maximum, please?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The first is, as part of my original Parliamentary Question, what other options and alternatives were considered and why were they not taken?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is a certain impression given that maybe, even though we might approach other external parties for similar collaborations in the future, will we then suddenly decide that actually, we have had enough, we have benefited enough, we are going to forge ahead.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, I think that really ties into our academic standing and our reputation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First question: what other options have we considered?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, the President of NUS, Prof Tan Eng Chye had laid it out in his op-ed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are various options to consider but the most important thing is to remember what are the guiding considerations in deciding on any option.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One, to make sure that we develop a generation of students that are much more global in their perspective, much more able to apply interdisciplinary approach to problem-solving.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, we must make sure that we continue to learn from the best.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am personally not very taken by ranking per se, because even if a university is ranked high or low, there are elements in the university that we can learn from.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It does not mean that a highly ranked university is good for everything and another university that is not so highly ranked, there is nothing that we can learn.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I think we must take a very open approach to considering partnerships with others to make sure that we continue to learn from them and to take the best aspects from these partnerships.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the other hand, as I have mentioned, when we go into a partnership with any foreign universities, we must also bring value to other people and we cannot just copy on the basis that they are better for us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Even if we try to learn from others, we must be prepared and be confident to chart out our own way to have our own unique value propositions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that is how we will continue to go forward.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At this point in time, I do not think this partnership coming to its natural checkpoint, will have any implications for any of the other partnerships that we are in or exploring with others.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As I have mentioned in my Parliamentary Question reply, actually for every partnership, we have milestones to check to make sure that both parties find it mutually beneficial for both of us to continue that relationship.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And at times, when it comes to a natural conclusion, we must be prepared to chart our own way forward, develop our own unique value proposition so that we can even be more attractive to other partners who would want to work with us and that we must continue to work together.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: NUS is taking a bold step today for the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Minister what would the Minister define as success for NUS and the students, given its vision for its interdisciplinary education?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I usually try not to have more than three key performance indicators (KPIs) for the organisations that I work with.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What is my definition of success for NUS and what is my definition of success for NUS students?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would say three for NUS and three for the NUS students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, first is the quality of our students in being able to be an integrative force for the world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That we provide solutions in context for the world just as we provide for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, these are my three KPIs for NUS.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How do I consider whether NUS students are successful?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not measure NUS students' success just by how well they do for themselves in the type of income that they earn or the type of jobs that they get.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that is because simply, NUS takes in the best from every cohort.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And as a society, as a country, we expect them to perform well, perform way above the average.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But in my own sense, I would like to see the success of NUS students defined in three ways.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Number one, they define success beyond themselves for the country.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Number two, they define success beyond themselves for our people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Number three, they define success beyond themselves for our future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For NUS students to be individually successful, that is to be expected because they are the cream of the crop from every cohort in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we want them to have a sense whereby their definition of success is not just about they, themselves, but how they can help Singapore defy the odds of history and continue to be a shining beacon, not just in Southeast Asia, but across the world and in history.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Number two, we want NUS students not to only define their success of again how well they do for themselves, but how well they enable the rest who are less privileged, perhaps less talented than them, to come along so that we can forge one people together, we can forge a nation together, we can forge that solidarity together, notwithstanding the forces that threaten to pull us apart.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Last but not least, we hope that the NUS students' success will be defined by not just how successful they are in this generation but by how successful they enable the next generation to be, perhaps to be even more successful than this generation.
